sections.body:
The ocean is the huge body of salt water that covers most of our planet. If you drew the Earth as a ball, the water would be much bigger than the land. The ocean holds almost all the water on Earth, and it is one connected body of water, so a drop of water in the Pacific can end up in the Atlantic.

The sea is not one place. It is a set of layers, like floors in a house. At the top is the **sunlight zone**, where the sun still reaches the water. Below that is the **twilight zone**, where the light fades to blue and then to black. Below that is the **deep sea**, which is dark and very cold all year long.

Almost all the animals of the world live in the sea. Sea animals are of every shape and size, from a shrimp you could hold in one finger to a whale longer than a bus.

The sea is also the hardest place to explore. Scientists have drawn maps of the sea floor for only part of the ocean, and they have seen most of the animals that live in the sunlight zone. The deep sea is still mostly unknown, and new species are found there every year.

Life in the ocean depends on one small thing: the sun. Tiny plants and animals drift near the surface and make food with sunlight, and everything else in the sea eats them, directly or indirectly. Take away the sunlit surface, and the whole ocean would go hungry.

So the ocean is not empty water. It is the biggest living space on Earth, and every layer of it is busy.

By the end of this article you will know what lives in each part of the sea, the words scientists use for these animals and their homes, and how to stay safe when the water is in front of you.
examples: The ocean covers most of the Earth.
Fish live in the sunlight zone.
The deep sea is dark and very cold.
sections.heading: What is under the ocean?

sections.body:
Coral reefs are the busy towns of the sea. A coral reef is built by tiny animals called corals, which build a hard skeleton together, one tiny piece at a time. Fish with bright stripes live in the gaps, and a clownfish even keeps a sea anemone safe by cleaning it. Sea turtles graze on the coral like cows on grass.

Seagrass meadows are underwater grass forests. They sway in the current, they shelter young fish, and they help the water stay clean.

Jellyfish are soft and see-through. They have no brain, no bones and no heart, yet they swim, hunt and can sting. They float up and down with the water, almost like paper lanterns.

Octopuses are clever. They can change colour to match the rocks, squeeze through any hole that fits their head, and open jars. Each arm has its own little brain.

Sharks are not the monsters films make them. Most are harmless to people. They have a nose that can smell a drop of blood from far away, and some can feel the electric fields of other animals.

Whales are the biggest animals that have ever lived. The blue whale eats more krill in one day than any other animal eats in a year. Whales sing, and their song can travel for hundreds of kilometres underwater.

And in the deepest water, where no sunlight ever goes, animals make their own light. Many of them glow, and they have eyes like huge golden saucers.
examples: The clownfish lives in the coral reef.
The jellyfish has no bones and no heart.
The whale is the biggest animal of all.
sections.heading: Who lives where in the sea

sections.body:
Water is heavy, so moving in it is hard work. Every sea animal has a good solution.

A **fish** breathes with **gills**. Gills are thin red strands inside the head. The fish takes in water through its mouth, and the gills take the oxygen out of it. That is why a fish drowns on land: it has no lungs, and it cannot use the air.

A **whale**, a **seal** and a **dolphin** breathe with lungs, exactly like you. They have to come up to the surface to take a breath. A whale blows a spout of water when it exhales, and from far away you can tell a blue whale from a humpback by the shape of the spout.

To move, most sea animals use a **fin** to steer and a **tail** to push. A fish wiggles its tail from side to side. A sea turtle rows with its front flippers, like a rower in a boat. An octopus pushes out a jet of water and shoots backwards, and it can jet so fast that it seems to fly.

Some sea animals have no heavy bones at all. A **squid** has a soft body, and a **jellyfish** is mostly water. A **pufferfish** fills itself with water until it looks like a balloon, too big for most fish to swallow.

And **shells** work like armour. A **turtle** carries its house with it. A **hermit crab** has no shell of its own, so it moves into an empty one and carries that instead.
examples: The fish breathes with gills, not with lungs.
The whale comes up to breathe and blows a spout.
The turtle carries its shell like a house on its back.
sections.heading: How sea animals breathe and move

sections.body:
These four words help you talk about the sea the way a scientist does.

Ocean is the great body of salt water that covers most of the Earth. When people talk about the sea, they usually mean this one connected ocean.

A **habitat** is the place where an animal lives, and the things it needs there: food, water, air and somewhere to hide. The reef is the habitat of the clownfish. The open water is the habitat of the whale.

A **coral reef** is a structure built by coral animals, made of limestone, and full of holes for small fish to hide in. Coral grows very slowly. A reef you see today is made over thousands of years, and the living skin on top of it grows only a little each year.

Plankton are tiny living things that drift with the currents. Some drift near the surface and make food with sunlight. Others are animals that eat them. Whales eat huge amounts of plankton, and so do small fish, and so do the birds that nest on islands above the sea.

Two more words are worth knowing. **Marine** means belonging to the sea, so a marine biologist is a scientist who studies the sea. And **reef** means the shallow ridge where coral grows, which is why a coral reef is also called a reef.
examples: The ocean is one big sea, so its water goes round and round.
The reef is the habitat of the small fish.
The plankton drift with the current all day.
sections.heading: The words scientists use

terms.example: The ocean is one big connected sea, not many small ones.
terms.gloss: The one great body of salt water that covers most of the Earth.

terms.example: The reef is the habitat of the clownfish and the small fish.
terms.gloss: The place where an animal lives, with the food, water and shelter it needs there.

terms.example: The coral reef grows a little slower every year.
terms.gloss: A structure built by coral animals out of limestone, full of holes where small fish hide.

terms.example: The whale eats tonnes of plankton every day.
terms.gloss: Tiny living things that drift with the currents near the surface of the sea.

sections.body:
The sea looks calm and it is not. Waves and currents can move a person much faster than they can swim. There is a way to enjoy the water and stay out of trouble.

First, **swim where the lifeguard is watching**. Lifeguards count the people in the water and know where the rip currents are. A lifeguard will also tell you if the flags say it is not safe to swim.

Second, **learn what a rip current is**. It is a narrow stream of water flowing away from the shore, often beside a cliff or a jetty. If you get caught in one, do not fight it. Float, swim sideways to get out of it, and then swim back along the beach.

Third, **wear a float** if you are not a strong swimmer, and do not go alone. The water is deeper than it looks, and the sea floor drops away quickly.

Fourth, **do not swim when you are tired, cold or full of food**. A tired body cannot fight a wave.

And fifth, **leave the wildlife alone**. Never touch a jellyfish, a shell or a coral. Look, admire, and leave it where it is.
examples: I will swim near the lifeguard tower.
If I get caught in a rip current, I will float first.
I will look at the jellyfish, but I will not touch it.
sections.heading: How to stay safe in the sea
steps: Swim where the lifeguard is watching.
Learn what a rip current is and what to do in one.
Wear a float if you are not a strong swimmer, and never swim alone.
Do not swim when you are tired, cold or full of food.
Look at the wildlife and never touch it.

sections.body:
Some sea animals can hurt you badly, and most of them do it without any warning at all. So we keep our hands out of the water unless we know what we are touching.

Jellyfish have stings. Some are gentle, and some, like the box jellyfish, can be very dangerous. Their stings can still hurt long after the jellyfish has washed away.

Bluebottles, which are a kind of jellyfish, blow onto beaches and leave long strings of stings in the sand. People often step on them without seeing them.

Stonefish are the hardest fish to see. They lie still on the bottom, they look like stones, and the spines on their back can cause a lot of pain.

Cone shells are beautiful cones with a sharp point, and they can sting inside a shell that is not alive anymore. That is why shells must not be taken home.

Coral looks soft, but living coral is covered in tiny stinging cells, and a piece of it can stay painful for days. Coral also takes hundreds of years to grow, so taking a piece is stealing from the future.

The rule is simple: **look with your eyes, keep your hands out**. A curious child who never touches gets to see far more than a child who grabs.
examples: Please do not touch the jellyfish.
This shell is pretty, but I will leave it on the sand.
I will look at the coral, and I will not break a piece.
sections.heading: Sea creatures you must never touch

item.summary: The ocean covers most of our planet, and every part of it is full of life. After reading this you can name the animals that live in each zone of the sea, use the words scientists use for them, and stay safe when you visit the beach.
item.title: Life Under the Ocean
